pages.title: Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events

claims.text: In a collaborative meta-analysis of individual participant data from six primary prevention trials (95,000 individuals at low average risk, 660,000 person-years, 3554 serious vascular events), aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction.

evidence.quote: In the primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18%vs 0.23% per year, p<0.0001).

claims.text: In the same meta-analysis, the net effect of aspirin on stroke in primary prevention was not significant, and vascular mortality did not differ significantly (0.19% vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7).

evidence.quote: The net effect on stroke was not significant (0.20%vs 0.21% per year, p=0.4: haemorrhagic stroke 0.04%vs 0.03%, p=0.05; other stroke 0.16%vs 0.18% per year, p=0.08). Vascular mortality did not differ significantly (0.19%vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7).

claims.text: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 trials randomizing 164,225 participants without cardiovascular disease, aspirin use was associated with a significant reduction in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 0.89, 95% credible interval 0.84-0.95; absolute risk reduction 0.38%, number needed to treat 265).

evidence.quote: Aspirin use was associated with significant reductions in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 61.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265).

claims.text: In the ARRIVE trial of 12,546 patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event, the primary composite endpoint occurred in 269 (4.29%) patients on aspirin versus 281 (4.48%) on placebo (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81-1.13; p=0.6038).

evidence.quote: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038).

claims.text: In the Japanese Primary Prevention Project of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with atherosclerotic risk factors, the 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between aspirin and no aspirin (2.77% vs 2.96%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77-1.15; P = .54).

evidence.quote: The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54).

claims.text: In the ASPREE trial of 19,114 older adults without cardiovascular disease, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years with aspirin and 11.3 with placebo (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.83-1.08).

evidence.quote: After a median of 4.7 years of follow-up, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08).

claims.text: In the ASCEND trial of 15,480 adults with diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 [8.5%] vs 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.79-0.97; P=0.01).

evidence.quote: During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01).

claims.text: In the collaborative meta-analysis, aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds in primary prevention (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001), and the main risk factors for coronary disease were also risk factors for bleeding.

evidence.quote: Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001), and the main risk factors for coronary disease were also risk factors for bleeding.

claims.text: In the 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis, aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding compared with no aspirin (23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 1.43, 95% credible interval 1.30-1.56; absolute risk increase 0.47%; number needed to harm 210).

evidence.quote: Aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding events compared with no aspirin (23.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 16.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210).

claims.text: In ARRIVE, gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0.97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0.46%) in the placebo group (HR 2.11; 95% CI 1.36-3.28; p=0.0007).

evidence.quote: Gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0·97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0·46%) in the placebo group (HR 2·11; 95% CI 1·36-3·28; p=0·0007).

claims.text: In ASCEND, major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) in the aspirin group versus 245 (3.2%) in the placebo group (rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09-1.52; P=0.003), with most of the excess being gastrointestinal bleeding and other extracranial bleeding.

evidence.quote: In contrast, major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 245 (3.2%) in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.52; P=0.003), with most of the excess being gastrointestinal bleeding and other extracranial bleeding.

claims.text: In ASPREE, the rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (HR 1.38; 95% CI 1.18-1.62; P<0.001).

evidence.quote: The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001).

claims.text: The 2009 collaborative meta-analysis concluded that in primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value, as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds.

evidence.quote: In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds.

claims.text: The 2019 systematic review concluded that aspirin use in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding.

evidence.quote: The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding.

claims.text: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for primary prevention of cardiovascular events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit, and that initiating aspirin in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit.

evidence.quote: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit. The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit.

claims.text: The USPSTF recommends that the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin for primary prevention in adults aged 40 to 59 years with a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk be an individual one (C recommendation), and recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin in adults 60 years or older (D recommendation).

evidence.quote: The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one. Evidence indicates that the net benefit of aspirin use in this group is small. Persons who are not at increased risk for bleeding and are willing to take low-dose aspirin daily are more likely to benefit. (C recommendation) The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation).

claims.text: In the secondary prevention trials of the collaborative meta-analysis, aspirin allocation yielded a greater absolute reduction in serious vascular events (6.7% vs 8.2% per year, p<0.0001), with reductions of about a fifth in total stroke and in coronary events.

evidence.quote: In the secondary prevention trials, aspirin allocation yielded a greater absolute reduction in serious vascular events (6.7%vs 8.2% per year, p<0.0001), with a non-significant increase in haemorrhagic stroke but reductions of about a fifth in total stroke (2.08%vs 2.54% per year, p=0.002) and in coronary events (4.3%vs 5.3% per year, p<0.0001).

claims.text: In ASPREE, the risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01-1.29).

evidence.quote: The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29).

claims.text: In ASPREE, cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years, with cancer-related death in 3.1% of the aspirin group versus 2.3% of the placebo group (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10-1.56).

evidence.quote: Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years. Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56).

claims.text: In ARRIVE, there were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (160 [2.55%] in the aspirin group vs 161 [2.57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group).

evidence.quote: There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group).

claims.text: In ASCEND, there was no significant difference between the aspirin and placebo groups in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 [2.0%] vs 158 [2.0%]) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] vs 887 [11.5%]), with long-term follow-up for these outcomes planned.

evidence.quote: There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%]); long-term follow-up for these outcomes is planned.

pages.title: ARRIVE trial (aspirin in moderate cardiovascular risk)

claims.text: ARRIVE was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study done in seven countries, in which eligible patients were men aged 55 years and older or women aged 60 years and older with an average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded.

evidence.quote: ARRIVE is a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study done in seven countries. Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors. We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes.

claims.text: Patients in ARRIVE were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive enteric-coated aspirin tablets (100 mg) or placebo tablets once daily, with patients, investigators and others involved in treatment or data analysis masked to treatment allocation.

evidence.quote: Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) with a computer-generated randomisation code to receive enteric-coated aspirin tablets (100 mg) or placebo tablets, once daily. Patients, investigators, and others involved in treatment or data analysis were masked to treatment allocation.

claims.text: The primary efficacy endpoint of ARRIVE was a composite outcome of time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or transient ischaemic attack, and safety endpoints were haemorrhagic events and incidence of other adverse events analysed in the intention-to-treat population.

evidence.quote: The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite outcome of time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or transient ischaemic attack. Safety endpoints were haemorrhagic events and incidence of other adverse events, and were analysed in the intention-to-treat population.

claims.text: Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12,546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites, with a median follow-up of 60 months.

evidence.quote: Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites. Median follow-up was 60 months.

claims.text: In ARRIVE, the overall incidence of serious adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (1266 [20.19%] with aspirin vs 1311 [20.89%] with placebo), as was the overall incidence of adverse events (5142 [82.01%] vs 5129 [81.72%]).

evidence.quote: The overall incidence rate of serious adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (n=1266 [20·19%] in the aspirin group vs n=1311 [20·89%] in the placebo group. The overall incidence of adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (n=5142 [82·01%] vs n=5129 [81·72%] in the placebo group).

claims.text: In ARRIVE, the overall incidence of treatment-related adverse events was low but differed between groups (1050 [16.75%] with aspirin vs 850 [13.54%] with placebo; p<0.0001).

evidence.quote: The overall incidence of treatment-related adverse events was low (n=1050 [16·75%] vs n=850 [13·54%] in the placebo group; p<0·0001).

claims.text: ASCEND randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo.

evidence.quote: We randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo.

claims.text: The primary efficacy outcome of ASCEND was the first serious vascular event (myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, or death from any vascular cause, excluding any confirmed intracranial hemorrhage), and the primary safety outcome was the first major bleeding event (intracranial hemorrhage, sight-threatening bleeding event in the eye, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other serious bleeding).

evidence.quote: The primary efficacy outcome was the first serious vascular event (i.e., myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, or death from any vascular cause, excluding any confirmed intracranial hemorrhage). The primary safety outcome was the first major bleeding event (i.e., intracranial hemorrhage, sight-threatening bleeding event in the eye, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other serious bleeding).

claims.text: A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization in ASCEND, with a mean follow-up of 7.4 years.

evidence.quote: A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization. During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years

claims.text: ASCEND concluded that aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but also caused major bleeding events, with the absolute benefits largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.

evidence.quote: Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events. The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.

pages.title: ASPREE trial (aspirin in the healthy elderly)

claims.text: From 2010 through 2014, ASPREE enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or 65 years of age or older among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, randomly assigned to 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.

evidence.quote: From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. Participants were randomly assigned to receive 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.

claims.text: The primary end point of ASPREE was a composite of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability, and secondary end points included major hemorrhage and cardiovascular disease defined as fatal coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal or nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure.

evidence.quote: The primary end point was a composite of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability; results for this end point are reported in another article in the Journal. Secondary end points included major hemorrhage and cardiovascular disease (defined as fatal coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal or nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure).

claims.text: Of the 19,114 persons enrolled in ASPREE, 9525 were assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo, with a median of 4.7 years of follow-up.

evidence.quote: Of the 19,114 persons who were enrolled in the trial, 9525 were assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo. After a median of 4.7 years of follow-up

claims.text: In ASPREE, a total of 1052 deaths occurred during a median of 4.7 years of follow-up, and deaths were classified according to the underlying cause by adjudicators unaware of trial-group assignments.

evidence.quote: A total of 1052 deaths occurred during a median of 4.7 years of follow-up. The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29).

claims.text: ASPREE concluded that higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death, a result described as unexpected in the context of previous studies and to be interpreted with caution.

evidence.quote: Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death. In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution.

claims.text: The Japanese Primary Prevention Project was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007 and followed up for up to 6.5 years.

evidence.quote: The Japanese Primary Prevention Project (JPPP) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial. Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years, with last follow-up in May 2012.

claims.text: Patients in JPPP were randomized 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg/d or no aspirin in addition to ongoing medications, and a multidisciplinary expert panel blinded to treatment assignments adjudicated study outcomes.

evidence.quote:
A multidisciplinary expert panel (blinded to treatment assignments) adjudicated study outcomes.
INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg/d or no aspirin in addition to ongoing medications.

claims.text: The composite primary outcome of JPPP was death from cardiovascular causes (myocardial infarction, stroke, and other cardiovascular causes), nonfatal stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic, including undefined cerebrovascular events), and nonfatal myocardial infarction.

evidence.quote: Composite primary outcome was death from cardiovascular causes (myocardial infarction, stroke, and other cardiovascular causes), nonfatal stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic, including undefined cerebrovascular events), and nonfatal myocardial infarction.

claims.text: JPPP was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years based on likely futility.

evidence.quote: The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility.

claims.text: In JPPP, 56 fatal events occurred in each group; nonfatal stroke occurred in 114 patients in the aspirin group and 108 in the no aspirin group, nonfatal myocardial infarction in 20 versus 38, and undefined cerebrovascular events in 3 versus 5.

evidence.quote: In both the aspirin and no aspirin groups, 56 fatal events occurred. Patients with an occurrence of nonfatal stroke totaled 114 in the aspirin group and 108 in the no aspirin group; of nonfatal myocardial infarction, 20 in the aspirin group and 38 in the no aspirin group; of undefined cerebrovascular events, 3 in the aspirin group and 5 in the no aspirin group.

claims.text: In its 2022 recommendation statement, the USPSTF commissioned a systematic review on the effectiveness of aspirin to reduce the risk of CVD events, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality in persons without a history of CVD, and a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.

evidence.quote: To update its 2016 recommendation, the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) commissioned a systematic review on the effectiveness of aspirin to reduce the risk of CVD events (myocardial infarction and stroke), cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality in persons without a history of CVD.

claims.text: The USPSTF population for the aspirin recommendation is adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.

evidence.quote: Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding (eg, no history of gastrointestinal ulcers, recent bleeding, other medical conditions, or use of medications that increase bleeding risk).

lint.note: Direction of the cardiovascular benefit differs by population: the 2009 and 2019 meta-analyses report a significant reduction in serious vascular events, while ARRIVE (moderate risk), JPPP (older Japanese with risk factors) and ASPREE (older adults) found no significant reduction in their primary cardiovascular endpoints; ASCEND found a significant reduction in adults with diabetes. The trials differ in population, risk level and design.

ASCEND found no significant difference in gastrointestinal tract cancer or all cancers, whereas ASPREE reported cancer-related death in 3.1% with aspirin versus 2.3% with placebo (HR 1.31) and attributed higher all-cause mortality primarily to cancer-related death; ASPREE itself notes the result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution.
No document given reports the effect of aspirin on colorectal cancer incidence or mortality, although the USPSTF commissioned a review of that outcome.
